lines.text: TMS therapy can lift people out of severe depression.
Then they're sent home — alone.
Within a year, roughly one in three relapses.
And the warning signs? Nobody is watching.
Meet OtaPath: a warm walking companion for the fragile weeks after treatment.
No questionnaires. No streaks. No guilt.
Just tiny real-world quests — while voice, photos and movement quietly keep the care team in the loop.
Feature one: the map is the game.
Matti opens the app, meets his walking buddy, and finds a gentle quest prescribed by his own doctor.
Every step outside clears golden mist from his real neighborhood.
There's nothing to fail — only streets to rediscover.
Feature two: memory capsules.
At the park, he snaps one vivid thing and leaves a ten-second voice note.
Under the hood, OtaPath reads the pitch and energy of his voice, the color and light of his photo, and the richness of his words.
No forms. He just made a memory — pinned to the map.
Feature three: the clinician's side of the loop.
Dr. Lindqvist's dashboard had already flagged Matti's quiet slide.
Today's capsule pulls his curves back up.
She plays his voice note, prescribes his next quest, sends a warm check-in — and seconds later, it lands on his phone.
OtaPath never asks how you feel — it notices.
Every signal is compared to the patient's own baseline, and a learning loop tracks which places lift each person.
Built in a single hackathon: a real app, a real backend, a real closed loop.
OtaPath. From hospital discharge to lasting recovery — one small walk at a time.
Step outside. Feel brighter.
